reason: The sources provide enough multi-sourced facts to support a surprising story about UY Scuti's size revision.
story: Back in 1860, astronomers at the Bonn Observatory cataloged a faint star in the constellation Scutum, naming it BD-12 degrees 5055. Decades later, its flickering brightness revealed it was a variable star, earning it the name UY Scuti. In 2012, using the Very Large Telescope in Chile, astronomers calculated that UY Scuti had a staggering radius of 1,708 times that of the Sun. This massive size crowned it the largest known star in the universe, with a volume large enough to swallow Jupiter's orbit. However, its reign did not last. Newer measurements using the Gaia space telescope revised its distance closer to Earth, shrinking its official radius down to just 909 solar radii. Today, UY Scuti is no longer the biggest star known, proving that even the most colossal facts in astronomy can change when better data arrives.
angle: A star once crowned the largest known in the universe shrunk by nearly half when astronomers remeasured its distance.

claims.claim: UY Scuti was first cataloged in 1860 by astronomers at the Bonn Observatory.
UY Scuti is located in the constellation Scutum.
UY Scuti was originally designated as BD-12 degrees 5055.
UY Scuti is a pulsating variable star with a pulsation period of about 740 days.
UY Scuti's apparent magnitude swings between 8.29 and 10.56, making it invisible to the naked eye.
In 2012, Very Large Telescope (VLT) interferometry in Chile helped calculate an old radius estimate of 1,708 solar radii.
Based on the 2012 measurements, UY Scuti was widely described as the largest known star.
Newer Gaia data and recent studies place UY Scuti's updated radius at approximately 909 solar radii.
UY Scuti is losing mass at a rate of 5.8 x 10^-5 solar masses per year, creating a circumstellar envelope of dust.
UY Scuti's surface temperature is approximately 3,365 to 3,550 Kelvin.
UY Scuti's luminosity is approximately 124,000 times that of the Sun (with older estimates reaching 340,000).
UY Scuti is expected to eventually end its life in a core-collapse supernova, leaving behind a neutron star or black hole.

disputed: Distance estimates vary between historical models of about 9,500 light-years and Gaia-based measurements of around 5,871 light-years; scripts should attribute older values as previous estimates according to early models.

The exact radius and whether it ever held the absolute crown permanently versus other contenders like Stephenson 2-18 is debated; scripts should state it was widely considered the largest or among the largest known stars.
